newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul to cut spending on infrastructure, education.
newsitem.headline: Seoul to cut spending on infrastructure, education.

text.p: South Korea will scale back public spending next year under an austerity budget designed to curb demand and reduce a ballooning current account deficit, the finance ministry said on Tuesday.
Budget growth next year will be capped at about nine percent, against a 13.4 percent rise in 1997 and 14.8 percent growth in 1996, the ministry said.
"The aim of the tight budget is to reduce a snowballing current account deficit and keep inflation in check," said Ha Sung, director at the ministry's state budget division.
"Infrastructure projects, loosely linked to improving industrial competitiveness, will be delayed," he said.
He said a cut in spending on education and agriculture was inevitable to meet new budget targets.
"All these sectors are politically sensitive areas. But a concensus on a tighter budget will be reached given the slowing economy," he said.
The ministry estimated next year's real economic growth at five to six percent, against a forecast 5.5 percent rise in 1997 and a 7.1 percent growth in 1996.
Analysts said the tighter budget would help reduce private-sector consumption and in turn lead to a cut in imports.

"The government's initiative is critical in trimming down unnecessary spending," said Shin Hoo-shik, an economist at the Daewoo Research Institute. He said he believed the government would easily meet its budget target.
He said consumer inflation could flare up unless the current account deficit was effectively controlled. Inflation is being stoked by a falling won, which makes imports more expensive.
The deficit this year is officially forecast at about $18 billion, down from a record $23.72 billion shortfall in 1996.
The ministry said next year's consumer price index was expected to rise between 4.0 and 4.5 percent, against a 4.5 percent growth in 1996.
Budget spending, including special accounts, was originally set to increase to about 71 trillion won ($79.9 billion) this year from 63 trillion won in 1996.
However, last Thursday finance minister Kang Kyong-shik told a news conference the government would slash tax revenues and spending by two trillion won this year.
Analysts said tax revenues would slow naturally as a result of an economic slowdown.
President Kim Young-sam earlier said about 10,000 jobs in the government offices would be slashed as part of measures to improve the international balance of payments.
A cyclical downturn in South Korea's key export industries, including semiconductors and ships, and the Japanese yen's steep fall against the U.S. dollar are behind the deficit.
The ministry said a final budget would be sent to the National Assembly for screening and approval by December 2 after cabinet approval. (Conversion $1 = 888.70)
